Time is not experienced uniformly; it is filtered through the body, the calendar, and the imagination. Each stage of life rearranges that filter — changing how fast time seems to pass, how much of it we believe remains, and how vividly death sits at the edge of awareness.

**Childhood: time as an endless present.** For a young child, time is largely episodic. Memory is sparse before roughly age three, and the "reminiscence bump" of early adulthood means most of what will later feel like *the story of a life* has not yet been laid down. A year is a fifth of everything the child has known, so summers stretch. Novelty is constant — first snow, first loss of a tooth — and novelty is what makes time feel dense in retrospect. Death is usually an abstraction, encountered first as absence or euphemism; children grasp its finality gradually, often through a pet or a grandparent.

**Adolescence: time as a stage to be escaped.** The future becomes vivid and urgent. Adolescents can imagine themselves far ahead but feel trapped in the present, which produces the characteristic impatience of the age. Mortality awareness sharpens into something personal and sometimes romanticized — the sense that one is invulnerable, or that dying young would be meaningful. Identity is being assembled, and time is the raw material: "who will I become" is a question about the future tense.

**Young adulthood: time as an expanding account.** This is when time feels most abundant and least examined. The proportional theory of time perception — a year is a smaller fraction of your life each birthday — predicts acceleration, but the sheer density of firsts (careers, loves, moves, children) counteracts it. Mortality is cognitively known but emotionally distant; death belongs to the old. The horizon feels open, and planning extends decades out. Many people discover only later that this was the period in which the *narrative* of their life was mostly written.

**Middle age: time as a dwindling, measurable resource.** Somewhere in the thirties or forties, the arithmetic flips. Instead of counting years since birth, people begin counting years left. Time stops being a bank balance and becomes a budget. This is when the "midlife" reckoning arrives — not merely a crisis of status but a confrontation with finitude: the realization that some doors have closed permanently, that parents are aging, that the body has begun its slow negotiation with gravity. Mortality shifts from an abstract fact to a felt trajectory. Awareness of death at this stage often produces either paralysis or a clarifying urgency — the "if not now, when."

**Old age: time as a narrowing present and a lengthening past.** Subjectively, time can speed up (each year a smaller fraction) even as days slow down (less novelty, more routine). The past becomes disproportionately large and vivid; the future shrinks to a short horizon. Yet studies of older adults reveal a paradox: emotional well-being often *improves*, and death anxiety frequently declines. Having survived losses, many elderly people report a kind of acceptance — a shift from "time left" to "time as it is." Reminiscence becomes a form of meaning-making, integrating a life into a coherent whole.

**Two cross-cutting ideas.** First, **Erikson's stages** frame the arc as a sequence of tasks — trust, identity, intimacy, generativity, integrity — each a different relationship to time: trusting the future, claiming a past, investing in what outlasts you, and finally accepting the whole. Second, **terror management theory** suggests that much of human culture — legacy, religion, art, children — is a response to mortality salience, and that this response is loudest when death feels near. The stages of life are, in this reading, a series of adjustments to the same underlying fact.

**The through-line** is that our sense of time and mortality is relational, not fixed. It depends on how much life we think we have behind us, how much novelty we encounter, and how close death feels — and all three shift as we age. The child lives in an expanding present, the adolescent in a charged future, the adult in a measured budget, the elder in a rich and narrowing now.
